catalog_quote: As in most languages, stress is a criterion for phonological word, since each word has just one syllable with primary stress. Chamacoco has intensity stress, whose scope is the single word, but it is mostly on the penultimate syllable. In disyllabic words, stress on the last syllable is relatively frequent, although also here stress on the penultimate is more common. One can identify some minimal pairs distinguished by stress (Ulrich and Ulrich 1994). [...] (20) [...] c. kasɨ-t /'kasɨt/ ~ kasɨ-t /ka'sɨt/ game-M.SG.AF ~ fearful-M.SG.AF 'Old Chamacoco game' ~ 'Fearful' [...] Stress can change depending on the context. For instance, since stress tends to be on the penultimate syllable, its position can change along with the syllable number in inflected forms of the word (21a). This is however a tendency which is not always observed (21b). Clitics, such as =ɨhɨ in (22a), can be stressed, and adding a clitic can change the accent position (22). [...] The possibility to carry stress applies to all clitics and elements cliticized at the right periphery of a word (cf. ex. 63-64 and 69-70).

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary (intensity) stress per phonological word, predominantly on the penultimate syllable; in disyllables final stress is fairly common but penult still prevails. Stress is phonologically distinctive in a small number of minimal pairs (e.g. 'kasɨt 'old game' vs ka'sɨt 'fearful'; 'ana 'this' vs a'na 'you laugh'). Stress tends to re-align to the penult when suffixes/clitics add syllables (al̥ɨbe → aˈl̥ɨbɨta; ˈlɨrk + =ɨhɨ → lɨrˈk=ɨhɨ), but not always (ˈn̥ote → ˈn̥otɨta). Ciucci 2016 (following Ulrich & Ulrich 1989b: 15) phrases the same pattern as a tendency (final in disyllables, penult in longer words) and adds that accent location varies from speaker to speaker and within one speaker's productions; accent is not written in the orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; source states each word has just one syllable with primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables with final stress (relatively frequent); lexically contrastive minimal pairs (ex. 20a-d in Ciucci 2020; fn. 90, 124, 339 in Ciucci 2016 list further verb pairs, e.g. [tɨkɨ'naˀ] 'to thank' vs [tɨ'kinaˀ] 'to laugh'); inflected forms that keep the stem stress instead of shifting to the penult (21b); clitics at the right periphery can take stress (22); Ciucci 2016: 59-60 notes inter- and intra-speaker variation in accent location.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: the domain is the single phonological word including right-edge clitics (Ciucci 2020 uses stress as a phonological-word criterion). Chamacoco is not tonal (Ciucci 2016: 60 fn. 52: 'Tones do not seem to have phonematic status'); word-final glottalization/laryngealization is a separate contrastive suprasegmental. Reading 'fixed: penultimate syllable' is a provisional label for a dominant tendency with lexical exceptions; 'lexical (unpredictable)' would be the alternative label if the minimal pairs and speaker variation are weighted more heavily.
new_statements.identity_note: Ciucci's descriptions (2013, 2016, 2020) refer to the Ebitoso (Ɨbɨtoso) dialect, spoken by the large majority of Chamacoco (Ciucci 2016: 'The data reported in this work refer to the Ɨbɨtoso dialect'; Ciucci 2020: 'Chamacoco has two dialects: Ebitoso and Tomaraho. I will refer to the former'). Glottolog cham1315 lists no separate dialect codes; the Tomárâho variety is not described for stress in anything opened.
